title: Italic Text (i)
description: The i element for an alternate voice or tone in text, and i vs em.
subject: html
html:
The <i> tag renders text in italics to mark an alternate voice or mood — technical terms, foreign phrases, ship and book names, or a character's internal thoughts — without adding any emphasis.

Syntax

<i>text to italicize</i>

Basic Example

<p>In SQL, a <i>subquery</i> is a query nested inside another query.</p>

Browser output: the word "subquery" renders in italics — flagging it as a technical term being introduced, not as a word the reader should stress when speaking the sentence aloud.

How It Works

The browser applies font-style: italic by default. Like <b>, this is a narrow, defined use case in HTML5: text set apart in a different "voice" from the surrounding prose, with no implied stress or importance.

Important Attributes

AttributePurpose
— none —Only universal global attributes apply

Real-World Example

<p>She kept thinking, <i>what if I missed the deadline?</i>, all through the meeting.</p>

Marking an internal thought as visually distinct from spoken dialogue or narration is a textbook <i> use case in fiction writing.

Comparison: i vs em

<i><em>
MeaningAlternate voice/tone — technical terms, foreign words, thoughts, titlesStress emphasis that can change a sentence's meaning
Default lookItalicItalic (visually identical)
If read aloudNo change in vocal stress impliedThe emphasized word would be stressed
ExampleThe ship <i>Titanic</i> sank in 1912.I <em>never</em> said she took it.

See emphasis for the full breakdown.

Common Mistakes

  • Using <i> when the intent is actually emphasis that changes meaning — that belongs in <em>
  • Reaching for <i> purely because "italics look nice" here, with no real alternate-voice justification

Best Practices

  • Use <i> for named categories of text: technical terms on first use, foreign-language phrases, taxonomic names, ship/book/film titles
  • Use <em> whenever stress genuinely changes what the sentence means

Accessibility Considerations

Like <b>, <i> carries no guaranteed special announcement in screen readers — some may apply a tonal change, but it isn't consistent or relied upon the way <em>'s emphasis behavior is.

SEO Considerations

No direct ranking effect from italicizing text with <i>.

Browser & Modern HTML Notes

Like <b>, HTML5 kept <i> but redefined its meaning away from pure presentation toward this "alternate voice" use case, rather than deprecating it.

Mini Practice

  1. Write a sentence introducing a technical term for the first time, italicized correctly with <i>.
  2. Write one sentence using <i> correctly and one that should really use <em> instead, and explain the difference.
